summary: In early September 2018 storms in Texas caused power swells that affected the cooling systems of Azure's South Central US data center. Temperatures rose, automated shutdown began and some hardware was damaged. Services including Visual Studio Team Services were down for many hours.

overview.background: The South Central US data center in San Antonio switched from utility to generator power during storms. Surge suppressors were in place, but the power swells still affected mechanical cooling.
systems: South Central US data center cooling and power
Azure compute and storage in the region
Visual Studio Team Services (now Azure DevOps)
Geo-redundant storage and SQL backups in a second region
overview.impact: One South Central US data center went offline. Visual Studio Team Services had its longest outage in seven years, and teams globally lost a day or more of productivity.
overview.severity: A multi-hour regional event with global effects on one service.
overview.gaps: The report used here is a news article about Microsoft's blog post. It gives no exact times.

timeline.e: Storms produce lightning and power swells in the Texas area.
The data center switches from utility to generator power. Mechanical cooling is affected by the swells.
Temperatures rise past safe thresholds and an automated shutdown begins. Some hardware is damaged.
Microsoft weighs failover to read-only secondary copies or restored backups against data loss, and waits for the region to recover.
Services in the region are restored.
A Microsoft DevOps engineering post describes the incident and next steps.

rootCause.trigger: Lightning-related power swells affected the data center's mechanical cooling systems.
rootCause.underlying: The data center kept running while temperatures rose until an automated shutdown, and temperatures rose so quickly that some hardware was damaged before shutdown.
contributing: Services were concentrated in one region
A regression made Dashboards unavailable when a Marketplace call failed
Service-to-service circuit breakers were scoped too widely, including calls to the user service
Failing over would have caused degraded service or data loss

evidence.label: Impact
evidence.body: lost a day or more of productivity

evidence.label: A simulated cooling alarm chain
evidence.body:
alert: ChillerFault
for: 2m
actions: [page-facilities, shed-noncritical-load, prepare-failover]
evidence.note: Invented example of an early action list.

diagnose.step: Check power quality and cooling status at the facility.
Check what your service replicates to other regions.

correct.step: Decide failover versus waiting using data loss risk.
correct.why: Microsoft waited because failover risked data loss.

correct.step: Restore in order: power, cooling, hardware, services.

prevent.step: Rehearse failover with your own organization first.

fix.safety: Failing over to an older copy can lose recent data. Decide the acceptable loss in advance.

troubleshoot.scenario: Cooling units trip after lightning and the room is heating. Your service has one region plus backups in another.
clues: The status page may be slow
troubleshoot.question: How do you decide?
troubleshoot.answer: Shed load, estimate recovery time against the data loss from failover, communicate regularly and choose by agreed recovery objectives.

rootcause.why: The report says swells affected mechanical cooling.

remediation.answer: Write acceptable data loss and recovery time per service.
Fail the service over in a test organisation first, then in production.
Break per dependency, not per call chain.

design.prompt: Design a service that survives a data center loss without losing data.
design.answer: Use zones, synchronous replication within a region, asynchronous across regions, rehearsed failover and tooling in two regions.

checks.q: Which service had its longest outage?
Why not fail over at once?
options: It would degrade services or lose data
They did not prevent the effect on cooling
checks.why: The report says swells affected cooling despite them.
